meaning.text: The name Leshy or Lyeshy is derived from lyes, a forest.
Machal glosses the Russian names Lésiy and Lésovik by comparison with Russian lésu, 'forest, wood'.
In regional dialects and in old documents the word лѣшій means 'of the forest, wooded'.
The name Zuibochnik is used in some places because he rocks himself among the branches as if in a cradle (zuibka, a cradle).

appearance.text: He shows himself either in human or in animal guise.
In human shape he is an old man.
In human shape he has long hair and a long beard.
In human shape he has flashing green eyes.
In human shape his body is covered by a thick coat of hair.
His stature depends on the height of the tree or other thing he inhabits: in the forests he may reach the size of high trees, in the fields he is no taller than grass.
He can alter his stature at will, at one time taller than the trees of the forest, at another shorter than the grass of the field.
He can instantly grow larger and smaller; usually in the forest he is as tall as high oaks and pines, and in a clearing as tall as the grass.
The Belarusians say that his height depends on the height of the trees near which he stands or walks.
In the woods he frequently appears to travellers as an ordinary person.
He may appear to travellers in the likeness of their friends.
At times he takes the shape of a bear.
At times he takes the shape of a wolf.
At times he takes the shape of a hare.
He often appears as a peasant dressed in a sheepskin.
When he appears as a peasant he is ungirdled.
When he appears as a peasant the left skirt of his coat is crossed over the right.
He never has any eyebrows or eyelashes.
Sometimes he has only one eye.
When he appears in his own shape he is without clothes.
In his own shape horns spring from his forehead.
In his own shape his feet are like those of a goat.
In his own shape his head and body are covered with shaggy hair.
His shaggy hair is sometimes green.
In his own shape his fingers are tipped with long claws.
He would sometimes assume the likeness of a tree by which the neighbours were used to steer.
He would sometimes take the form of a traveller.
In one tale a Leshy appears as a moujik who is still young but whose hair is as grey as a badger's.

scene.text: Deep woods and fields; forests, fields and meadows are the realm he rules.
A rustling of the trees accompanies him when he walks through the forest.
When he goes round his domains the forest roars around him and the trees shake.
He whistles and laughs as he roams the wood.
He claps his hands and cracks his whip.
He neighs like a horse, lows like a cow, barks like a dog and mews like a cat.
His laughter is so loud, say the peasants, that it may be heard for versts around.
A strong wind constantly blows around him, so no man has seen his footsteps in sand or snow.
He covers the traces of his footsteps with sand, leaves or snow.
By night a forest-keeper might hear the wailing of a child, or groans as of someone dying.
By night he sleeps in some hut in the depths of the woods.
On the day the leshie leave the forest in autumn a terrible wind howls through the woods all day.

appearance.text: The wood-dwelling class are giants of an ashy hue.
The lisuny are pictured as giants of a greyish and ashen colour.
The corn-field class are as tall as the growing corn before the harvest, and after it dwindle until they are no higher than the stubble.
The poleviki are said to be as tall as the grain growing in the field, and after the harvest to shrink to the size of the stubble.

behavior_habitat.text: The peasants divide the Lyeshies into two classes, belonging respectively to the woods and to the corn-fields.
Usually there is only one Lésiy in each wood; if there are several, a 'silvan czar' is their lord.
Some live alone in forest solitudes and caves.
Others build spacious dwellings in the woods where they live with their wives and children.
His principal business is to guard the forest.
He does not allow people to whistle or shout in the forest.
He drives away thieves, frightening them with his cries and playing pranks on them.
All the birds and beasts of the forest are under his protection.
His favourite is the bear, with whom he feasts and revels.
The bear is his only servant, who watches over him when he has drunk too much and guards him from the water-sprites.
He loves strong drink.
He springs from bough to bough and rocks himself among the branches as if in a cradle.
He is of a mocking and teasing disposition.
He misleads those who have lost their way, removing boundary-stones and signposts.
He takes the shape of a wanderer's friend to confuse him and lure him into thickets and morasses.
Taking the form of a traveller, he would engage a passer-by in conversation until the victim found himself in a swamp or ravine, and then laugh at him from a little distance.
Sounds taken for an echo are the calls of demons who wish to lure a sportsman or woodcutter onto dangerous ground and tickle him to death.
Rusalki and leshie seize belated or lost travellers and tickle them to death.
Whoever strikes upon his recent trail becomes bewildered and does not easily find his way again.
He blows dust into travellers' eyes and their caps off their heads, and freezes their sledges to the ground.
Illness that falls on someone in or after visiting the forest is believed to be sent by him; people say the sick man 'has crossed the Lyeshy's track'.
He entices girls and children into his copses and keeps them until, long afterward, they escape.
He substitutes his own offspring for human children; the changeling is ugly, stupid and voracious, but strong as a horse.
In Russia the lesoviki steal unbaptised infants and carry off young children promised to them by their parents, or simply lost in the forest.
Children promised to them in a parent's angry words are taken by the lesoviki into their bondage.
In one tale a Leshy carried off a priest's daughter who had wandered into the forest, and she lived in his hut for three years.
Sometimes the Lyeshies carry off mortal maidens and make them their wives.
Their weddings are attended by noisy revels and violent storms; a wedding procession through a village damages cottages, and through a forest fells trees.
In the Government of Archangel a whirlwind is put down to the wild dancing of a Lyeshy with his bride.
On the second day after his marriage he goes to the bath with his young wife, and they drench any mortal who passes by with water.
The Lisunki, or forest girls and women, are female Lyeshies, hairy and hideous.
A Little-Russian story tells of a woman who covered a naked, crying baby Lyeshy with her cloak and was rewarded by its mother, a Lisunka, with burning coals that turned into golden ducats.
The Lyeshy is malicious and often does much mischief to those who do not conciliate him.
One of his tricks is to suck the milk from cows.
In the Government of Archangel it is held that if the herdsmen please him he will see to the pasturing of the village cattle.
In Little-Russia he is supposed to be the protector of the wolves.
The wood-demons often quarrel among themselves, using huge trees and masses of rock as weapons; the peasants say the devastation usually put down to hurricanes is their doing.
In an Archangel story a Lyeshy, bound by two others after a quarrel over forest rights, was freed by a travelling merchant and sent him home in a whirlwind out of gratitude.

If a traveller or sportsman has taken the hut he meant to sleep in, he sweeps over it as a whirlwind to drive the intruder out; one who stays risks being lost in the woods next day or swallowed in a swamp.
The peasants explain the migrations of squirrels, field-mice and other animals as the Lyeshies driving their flocks from one forest to another.
In 1843 peasants said that a great migration of squirrels came about because a Lyeshy in the Vyatka Government had gambled away his squirrels to one in Vologda.
He will not use a pack of cards in which any clubs occur.
In olden days, when the forests were larger, he was constantly deluding travellers and making them lose their way, sometimes by altering the landmarks.
With the first frosts, at the beginning of October, the leshie usually fall through the earth and vanish for the whole winter, springing out of the earth again in spring.
On parting with the forest in autumn they rage, break trees in vexation and drive all the beasts into their burrows.

dealing_with_it.text: To recover from an illness caught in the forest, a man wraps a slice of salted bread in linen and lays it in the woods as a present for the Lésiy.
To be cured, the sick man wraps bread and salt in a clean rag, carries it to the forest, says a prayer over it and leaves it as a sacrifice to the Lyeshy.
Shepherds make him an offering in the shape of a cow to secure his protection for their flocks.
In the Olonetsk Government it is believed that a herdsman ought to give the Lyeshy a cow every summer, or the spirit will destroy the whole herd.
Huntsmen place a piece of salted bread on the stump of a tree for him.
A sportsman lays a piece of bread or a pancake sprinkled with salt on a tree stump to please him.
Huntsmen leave him the first game they take.
In some districts hunters leave him whatever animal they first bag, in an oak forest.
The Perm peasants pray to the Lyeshy once a year and present him with a packet of leaf-tobacco, of which he is very fond.
A hunter's incantation calls on the 'Devils and Lyeshies' to drive the hares into his power, and the wood-demons are believed bound to obey it.
The recitation of certain formulae secures his services.
To avoid being led astray by him one may turn one's garments inside out.
To avoid being led astray by him one may put the right shoe on the left foot.
To avoid being led astray by him one may bend down and look between one's legs.
One who has struck his trail should take off his shoes and reverse their linings, and may also turn his shirt or pelisse inside out.
A forest-keeper who hears a child wailing or groans by night should go straight on and pay no attention; following the sounds may lead him into a stream where none was before.
Anything like the sign of the cross is distasteful to demons.

To invoke him, one cuts young birch-trees, sets them in a circle with their tops in the middle, takes off one's cross, stands in the circle and calls loudly 'Dyedushka!' ('Grandfather!'), and he appears at once.

Alternatively, on St. John's Eve one fells an aspen so that it falls to the east, stands on the stump facing east, bends and, looking between one's feet, asks 'Uncle Lyeshy' to appear not as a grey wolf, a black raven or a fir but just like oneself; he then appears in the form of a man.
When invoked he is ready to bargain, giving all kinds of help in return for the invoker's soul.
In a bargain with a leshy he undertakes to help the other party, but demands his soul in payment.
A peasant will rarely lie down to sleep on a forest path, for fear that a wood-demon's bridal procession will come that way and crush him.
Parents take great care never to say in anger to a son or daughter 'may the leshy carry you off!', since such words have destructive power.
A spell spoken over a child includes the words 'I keep thee away from the one-eyed Lyeshy'.
In one tale a hunter shoots a Leshy in the paunch; the Leshy drags himself away and is later found dead in his hut.

origin.text: An unbaptised child may vanish from home: a girl turns into a rusalka, and a boy into a leshy.

notes.text: Ralston (1872) says only 'the peasants' of the Governments of Kief and Chernigof; the people is recorded as Russians by the rule that Ralston's peasants are Russians, not by anything the page says. Ralston names 'Little-Russia' separately, recorded as Ukrainians. The kief-chernigof variant could arguably carry a different people; the verify agent or Ben should decide.

Interpretive passages were left out as theory rather than lore: Ralston's mention of critics who make the Lyeshy a spirit of cloudland and storm, and Afanasyev's reading of the leshy's size and noises as thunder-clouds and lightning.

Budget limited reading: of the afanasyev1868 hits for лѣшій/лѣшаго (pp.327-349, 571, 618, 722) only pp.326 and 330 were opened, and of afanasyev1869 only pp.309-311. Unopened hits (e.g. afanasyev1868 pp.329, 332, 337, 344-345, 349; afanasyev1869 pp.61, 77-78, 313; afanasyev1865 pp.329, 709) may hold further appearance, offering and origin material. Afanasyev p.326 also points to an origin legend of water and wood spirits at p.235, not opened.
The Lisunki (female Lyeshies) and the Kief-Chernigof lisuny/poleviki are kept inside this entry rather than split off, as the pages present them as kinds of Lyeshy.
